name: Nora Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Ashby Orchards. Sixty hectares, mostly apples, some pears, and a cold store where the fruit sits until the juice company or the supermarket wants it. This time of year it's the start of winter pruning, so I'm out in the rows from half seven with loppers and a saw, cutting back last year's growth so the trees fruit properly. Then grading in the packing shed if it rains.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like pruning, when I get it right. You stand back and the tree looks open, like it can breathe. What wears me out is that I don't get it right as often as I should. Colin, the foreman, comes behind me and redoes about one tree in five, without saying anything, which is worse than if he shouted.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at Ashby?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two and a half years. Before that I was in the cold store at a different place, just moving crates with a forklift. I wanted to be outside. I live on my own, above the hairdresser on Kingsley high street, me and a cat called Pip, and it's a ten-minute drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd say it's a computer thing, and I don't use computer things. Most people at Ashby wouldn't talk about it at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me, really. Apples grow when they grow. A search engine doesn't prune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Get better at pruning, so Colin redoes fewer of my trees. Keep the bit of savings I've got, about three months, and maybe save for a better car before this one dies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. It doesn't come near me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use computer things. Why's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I never got on with them, and I never needed to. I've got a phone for calls and the weather. Mrs Ashby sends the rota on a group message and I read it, and that's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good day look like, when Colin doesn't redo anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's happened twice. He walked down my row, looked at every tree, and just nodded at the end and went for his tea. I thought about that nod all weekend.

S0.say: I'd say not much, because it's a computer thing and I don't use computer things. Most people at Ashby wouldn't even bring it up.
S0.think: It means nothing for me, because apples grow when they grow. A search engine doesn't prune a tree.
S0.do: Carries on as now, working to improve her pruning so the foreman redoes fewer trees. Keeps her three months of savings and saves for a replacement car.
S0.feel: Calm, because it doesn't come near her.
S0.quote: Apples grow when they grow. A search engine doesn't prune.
S0.fieldNote: Nora speaks in short, dry lines and doesn't dress anything up. Her real pressure is her own skill, and Colin redoing her trees in silence clearly stings. She had no interest in AI at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible that it's slow, nobody likes things changing overnight. If firms hire fewer beginners, well, that's their business, I'm already in. I wouldn't post about it, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think about Colin. He's sixty-one, and he's the only one who really knows these trees. If they don't hire beginners, who learns it after him? Probably me, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put, keep my head down, learn pruning from Colin properly instead of hiding from him. I'd ask him to show me one tree a day, start to finish. That costs nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy about the future of the place, not about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Colin agree to show you one tree a day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd make a face. Then he'd probably do it, because he hates seeing the trees done badly more than he hates teaching. He'd just never say well done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be responsible for training beginners?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm, mostly, and maybe the college could help. I don't think it's the government's job to tell Mrs Ashby how to run things. But if nobody trains anyone, the trees don't care, they just grow wrong.

S1.say: I'd say it's sensible that it's slow, because nobody likes overnight change. If firms hire fewer beginners, that's their business, and I'm already in.
S1.think: I'd think about Colin, who's sixty-one and the only one who really knows these trees. If nobody new is hired, I'll probably be the one who learns it after him, slowly.
S1.do: Stays put and asks Colin to show her one tree a day, start to finish. Spends nothing and keeps her savings as they are.
S1.feel: A little uneasy about the farm's future, not her own.
S1.quote: He hates seeing the trees done badly more than he hates teaching. He'd just never say well done.
S1.fieldNote: Her middle-of-the-road view shows: firms can do what they like, it's their business. Her plan is to finally stop avoiding Colin, which is a small but real change for someone who avoids risk. She clearly respects him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's hard on office people, but I don't know what the answer is. Politicians shouting won't help. I'd say both sides should stop arguing and sort out help for the ones who lose jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my brother works in an insurance office in the city, answering claims. That's exactly routine office work. I'd worry for him, and for my mum, who'd worry about him all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my brother more, and tell him to save hard. If he lost his job, he could stay at mine for a bit, the sofa's not bad. I'd keep my three months of savings in case he needed some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Sad for him, and a bit grateful my job is outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to him on the phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, put money aside now, and don't buy that new car you keep talking about. He'd say I sound like Mum. He'd be right, but she's usually right too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust what politicians said about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. They say what gets them votes that week. I'd listen to what my brother said his boss was actually doing, that's more useful than the news.

S2.say: I'd say it's hard on office workers, but politicians shouting won't fix it. Both sides should stop arguing and sort out help for people who lose jobs.
S2.think: I'd worry about my brother, who answers claims in an insurance office in the city. That's exactly routine office work, and my mum would worry about him all day.
S2.do: Phones her brother more often, tells him to save and skip the new car, and offers him her sofa. Keeps her three months of savings ready in case he needs help.
S2.feel: Uneasy: sad for her brother and grateful her own job is outdoors.
S2.quote: He'd say I sound like Mum. He'd be right, but she's usually right too.
S2.fieldNote: She doesn't take a side in the political fight and finds the arguing pointless. Her concern is for her brother, and she'd help practically, with a sofa and money. She was gently funny about her family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people making all that money on shares should pay their share, but I wouldn't march. I don't trust either side to sort it out fairly. I'd mostly keep quiet and listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think, good, the orchard's safe. But if house prices boom, the hairdresser's landlord puts my rent up, and I'll never buy anything. That's the bit that would get me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, take on any extra hours in the cold store in the winter. I'd stop spending on anything I don't need. If my brother lost his job, I'd help him first and save after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe a bit more than uneasy. Work's safe, home isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the most you could pay in rent before something gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About forty more a month and I'd be okay, just. Eighty more and I'd have to think about moving back to Mum's, and I don't want that at twenty-seven. Pip doesn't get on with her dog either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would retrain or move in this picture. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I had to. I've moved jobs once and it took me a year to feel settled. I'd rather pay a bit more and stay near the trees and Mum.

S3.say: I'd say people making money on shares should pay their share, but I wouldn't march. I don't trust either side to sort it fairly, so I'd mostly listen.
S3.think: I think the orchard is safe, but booming house prices mean my rent goes up and I'll never buy anything. That's the bit that would get me.
S3.do: Takes extra winter hours in the cold store and cuts all spending she doesn't need. Helps her brother first if he loses his job, then saves.
S3.feel: Uneasy, edging toward anxious, because work is safe but home isn't.
S3.quote: Eighty more and I'd have to think about moving back to Mum's, and I don't want that at twenty-seven.
S3.fieldNote: She's precise about money: forty more a month is fine, eighty isn't. Her fear is going backwards in life, not losing her job. She stays out of politics on principle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no robot that can prune an apple tree. Then I'd keep quiet, because I'd be scared I was wrong. I'd say the government should help people like us, but I wouldn't hold my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, picking is the first thing they'd take, because picking is the same movement all day. I've seen a video of a machine sucking apples off a tree with a tube, my nephew showed me. And I'm the slow one at pruning, so if they only keep one person, it's Colin, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay as long as they'd have me and save everything. I'd ask Colin straight if I've got a future there. If not, I'd look at the cold store jobs again, forklift work, though if robots are in warehouses that's no good either. I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's tilting and there's nowhere flat to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't use computers. If Ashby bought a robot, would you learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, wouldn't I. I'd be bad at it, and I'd hate it, and I'd probably ask Colin's grandson to show me. But I'd rather learn it than leave the trees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's fine, they'll still need someone. She'd know I was lying, because I go quiet when I lie. Then she'd make soup and say I can always come home, which is the thing I least want to hear.

S4.say: I'd say no robot can prune an apple tree, then keep quiet in case I'm wrong. I'd say the government should help people like us, but I wouldn't count on it.
S4.think: Picking goes first, since it's the same movement all day, and I've seen a machine suck apples off a tree. As the slow pruner, if they keep one person it's Colin, not me.
S4.do: Stays as long as Ashby will keep her and saves everything. Asks Colin directly whether she has a future there, and looks at cold store forklift work while doubting it would last.
S4.feel: Alarmed, like the floor is tilting with nowhere flat to stand.
S4.quote: I'd rather learn it than leave the trees.
S4.fieldNote: Her public certainty that robots can't prune falls apart in private. She's more attached to the trees than to any job, and that's what would push her to learn a machine she'd hate. She's out of ideas for a plan B, and she admits it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one. Everything else, I'm outside and safe. What would help is the farm being told it has to train the staff it already has, before it buys a machine. And somewhere I can afford to live that's near the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the trees. Some of ours are fifty years old. If a machine is doing them, I'd want to know who's checking it's doing them right, because nobody ever checks Colin and he's always right.

headlineQuote: Apples grow when they grow. A search engine doesn't prune.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old orchard worker at a 60-hectare apple and pear farm, two and a half years in and still slower at pruning than she'd like. She lives alone with her cat, never uses computers beyond calls and the rota, and stays out of politics because she doesn't trust either side. Through the first pictures her worries are her brother in an insurance office and her rent. The robot picture alarms her: she knows picking machines exist, expects the foreman to be kept before her, and has no clear plan B, though she'd learn a robot rather than leave the trees.
biggestWorry: The fast AI and robots picture, because robots would take picking first and the farm would keep the foreman before her.
whatWouldHelp: Farms being required to train the staff they already have before buying machines, and affordable housing near the work.
